name: Cryptographic Protocols
description: Design and analysis of cryptographic protocols such as TLS, key exchange, messaging, and PKI.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this collection, all from USENIX Security 2018, show a field already split between two recurring concerns: building new cryptographic systems and breaking or formally scrutinizing existing protocols. On the construction side, "Arbitrum: Scalable, private smart contracts" (USENIX 2018) pushed cryptographic machinery toward scalable, privacy-preserving computation, while on the attack side "The Dangers of Key Reuse: Practical Attacks on IPsec IKE" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that real-world key-establishment standards remained exploitable when keys were shared across modes. Alongside these, "Modelling and Analysis of a Hierarchy of Distance Bounding Attacks" (USENIX 2018) signaled an early commitment to formal, calculus-based reasoning about protocol security — a thread that would only grow stronger.

The next few years marked a clear breakthrough toward automated formal analysis of protocol families rather than one-off proofs. "A Spectral Analysis of Noise" (USENIX 2020) gave a comprehensive automated treatment of the entire Noise family of Diffie-Hellman handshakes, and "SmartVerif" (USENIX 2020) pushed automation further with dynamic verification strategies, while "Analysis of DTLS Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing" (USENIX 2020) brought systematic state-machine testing to deployed code. In parallel, the community kept finding that widely trusted deployments leak: "Why Eve and Mallory Still Love Android" (USENIX 2021) showed TLS validation was still broken in mobile apps, "Why TLS is better without STARTTLS" (USENIX 2021) and "ALPACA" (USENIX 2021) exposed cross-protocol and application-layer confusion attacks against TLS, and "Card Brand Mixup Attack" (USENIX 2021) bypassed PINs in EMV payment cards. Secure messaging matured into its own subfield, with "The Complexities of Healing in Secure Group Messaging" (USENIX 2021) formalizing post-compromise security across groups and "Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G" (USENIX 2021) hardening cellular authentication.

By 2022–2023 the work fused rigorous cryptanalysis with the messengers and databases people actually use. "Breaking Bridgefy, again" (USENIX 2022) showed that adopting libsignal does not automatically yield security, and "Three Lessons From Threema" (USENIX 2023) delivered a full cryptographic teardown of a ten-million-user messenger. The same period broadened the scope to encrypted databases and large-scale TLS hygiene, with "Security Analysis of MongoDB Queryable Encryption" (USENIX 2023) and "We Really Need to Talk About Session Tickets" (USENIX 2023) measuring real cryptographic dangers at scale, while "Linear Private Set Union" (USENIX 2023) advanced efficient privacy-preserving set operations.

Most recently the field has turned to the post-quantum transition and cross-chain settings while keeping its formal-methods backbone. "Formal verification of the PQXDH Post-Quantum key agreement protocol" (USENIX 2024) verified Signal's new post-quantum handshake before wide deployment — a direct descendant of the automated-analysis line begun around 2020 — and "Parallelizing Universal Atomic Swaps for Multi-Chain Cryptocurrency Exchanges" (USENIX 2025) extends secure-protocol design into trustless cross-blockchain exchange. Across these venues the trajectory is consistent: from isolated attacks and constructions, to automated analysis of whole protocol families, to rigorous study of mass-deployed messengers and databases, and now to post-quantum and multi-chain protocols verified before they ship.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work on this list is preoccupied with hardening the protocols the web already runs on. "TLS-N: Non-repudiation over TLS Enablign Ubiquitous Content Signing" (NDSS 2018) extends TLS so that a client can prove to a third party what a server actually sent, turning an ordinary session into signed, shareable evidence, while "Preventing (Network) Time Travel with Chronos" (NDSS 2018) shores up NTP, the quiet dependency that so many cryptographic deadlines and certificate checks rely on. The message of this period is that deployed protocols need auditability and robustness, not just confidentiality.

The next shift is toward rigorous, machine-checked analysis of the protocols that guard billions of devices. "Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA: Channel Assumptions and Session Confusion" (NDSS 2019) — by far the most cited paper here — used formal methods to expose subtle authentication flaws in the 5G standard before mass rollout, and "maTLS: How to Make TLS middlebox-aware?" (NDSS 2019) tackled the awkward reality that middleboxes routinely break end-to-end TLS. That formal-analysis thread deepened over the following years: "A Formal Analysis of the FIDO UAF Protocol" (NDSS 2021) scrutinized passwordless login, "Extrapolating Formal Analysis to Uncover Attacks in Bluetooth Passkey Entry Pairing" (NDSS 2023) and "Rediscovering Method Confusion in Proposed Security Fixes for Bluetooth" (NDSS 2025) kept finding pairing weaknesses, and "A Unified Symbolic Analysis of WireGuard" (NDSS 2024) brought the same rigor to a modern VPN. A complementary strand automated the hunt for implementation-level bugs, as in "Automata-Based Automated Detection of State Machine Bugs in Protocol Implementations" (NDSS 2023).

Alongside the verification work, the area broadened into the cryptographic machinery behind decentralized systems and privacy-preserving data services. Consensus and randomness became first-class protocol problems — "LaKSA: A Probabilistic Proof-of-Stake Protocol" (NDSS 2021), "NC-Max: Breaking the Security-Performance Tradeoff in Nakamoto Consensus" (NDSS 2022), and "OptRand: Optimistically Responsive Reconfigurable Distributed Randomness" (NDSS 2023) — while "Real Threshold ECDSA" (NDSS 2023) and payment-channel work like "Breaking and Fixing Virtual Channels: Domino Attack and Donner" (NDSS 2023) pushed threshold signatures and off-chain protocols forward. In parallel, searchable and private-computation primitives matured through "Practical Non-Interactive Searchable Encryption with Forward and Backward Privacy" (NDSS 2021) and "Obfuscated Access and Search Patterns in Searchable Encryption" (NDSS 2021). Internet-infrastructure PKI also got attention, with "BGP-iSec: Improved Security of Internet Routing Against Post-ROV Attacks" (NDSS 2024), "dRR: A Decentralized, Scalable, and Auditable Architecture for RPKI Repository" (NDSS 2024), and "Certificate Transparency Revisited: The Public Inspections on Third-party Monitors" (NDSS 2024).

The most recent work shows two clear frontiers. First, the quantum clock is now driving TLS design: "Looma: A Low-Latency PQTLS Authentication Architecture for Cloud Applications" (NDSS 2026) rebuilds TLS authentication around post-quantum primitives while fighting their latency cost, and "SoK: Cryptographic Authenticated Dictionaries" (NDSS 2026) and "CTng: Secure Certificate and Revocation Transparency" (NDSS 2026) systematize and modernize the PKI transparency layer. Second, the field keeps refining Byzantine consensus and private set operations at scale, seen in "Ipotane: Balancing the Good and Bad Cases of Asynchronous BFT" (NDSS 2026), "Icarus: Achieving Performant Asynchronous BFT with Only Optimistic Paths" (NDSS 2026), and "Faster Than Ever: A New Lightweight Private Set Intersection and Its Variants" (NDSS 2026). Fittingly, the 2018 idea of proving what a TLS session carried returns matured in "ACTS: Attestations of Contents in TLS Sessions" (NDSS 2026), now framed around Web3 data ownership — closing a loop from content signing on TLS to verifiable, attestable sessions.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection already splits along two lines that would define the area. One line attacks and formally scrutinizes deployed protocols: "DEEPSEC: Deciding Equivalence Properties in Security Protocols" (S&P 2018) pushed automated verification forward, "Distance-Bounding Protocols: Verification without Time and Location" (S&P 2018) formalized proximity guarantees, and "A Formal Treatment of Accountable Proxying Over TLS" (S&P 2018) reasoned about the middleboxes that inspect real Internet traffic. The other line builds the cryptographic machinery for distributed systems: "Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions" (S&P 2018) made threshold signing of a ubiquitous scheme practical, while "OmniLedger" (S&P 2018) showed how to shard a permissionless ledger at scale.

Through 2019-2021 both lines accelerated. On the attack side, "The 9 Lives of Bleichenbacher's CAT" (S&P 2019) revived a classic padding oracle against real TLS implementations, "Dragonblood" (S&P 2020) broke the freshly minted WPA3 handshake, "BIAS: Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS" (S&P 2020) impersonated paired devices, and "The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify" (S&P 2021) crystallized a break-fix-verify workflow on the global card-payment protocol. Meanwhile the blockchain-driven half exploded: payment channels and hubs in "Perun" (S&P 2019), "A2L" (S&P 2021), and "Bitcoin-Compatible Virtual Channels" (S&P 2021); consensus in "Sync HotStuff" (S&P 2020); proof-of-stake and interoperability in "Proof-of-Stake Sidechains" and "XCLAIM" (both S&P 2019); and the first randomness beacons such as "HydRand" (S&P 2020). "Post-quantum WireGuard" (S&P 2021) planted an early flag for the quantum-safe future.

By 2022-2023 the distributed-crypto toolkit matured and consolidated. "Practical Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation" (S&P 2022) removed timing assumptions from a core primitive, "Spurt" (S&P 2022) built a scalable beacon on a transparent setup, and "SoK: Distributed Randomness Beacons" (S&P 2023) stepped back to systematize the whole space. Threshold and privacy signing advanced with "Threshold BBS+ Signatures for Distributed Anonymous Credential Issuance" (S&P 2023), while "ProVerif with Lemmas, Induction, Fast Subsumption, and Much More" (S&P 2022) sharpened the verification tooling that the analysis line depends on.

The most recent papers show the area converging on two priorities: rigorous analysis of the messaging protocols people actually use, and the post-quantum migration. "Automated Formal Analysis of Signal's Double Ratchet" (S&P 2026) brings machine-checked attacks, fixes, and proofs to the heart of end-to-end encrypted messaging, echoing the earlier ProVerif and DEEPSEC verification thread. In parallel, a wave of quantum-safe constructions arrives: "A Maliciously-Secure Post-Quantum OPRF from Crypto Dark Matter," "Blinding Post-Quantum Hash-and-Sign Signatures," "Lattice-Based Threshold Blind Signatures," "Starfighters-On the General Applicability of X-Wing" on KEM combiners, and "Revisiting PQ Wireguard" (all S&P 2026), which returns to the 2021 design with a comprehensive security analysis. The threshold and asynchronous-systems line continues too, with "Practical Asynchronous Distributed Key Reconfiguration" and "Optimistic Asynchronous Dynamic-Committee Proactive Secret Sharing" (both S&P 2026). The field now runs from breaking real deployed handshakes to formally proving the fixes, all while re-founding its primitives on post-quantum assumptions.

ccs.narrative:
Cryptographic protocols at CCS cover the full stack from key exchange and messaging to consensus and PKI. The 2018 cohort was dominated by blockchain-adjacent protocol work: RapidChain: Scaling Blockchain via Full Sharding (CCS 2018) achieved the highest throughput of its time via complete sharding of communication, computation, and storage, while BEAT: Asynchronous BFT Made Practical (CCS 2018) and General State Channel Networks (CCS 2018) addressed consensus and off-chain scaling respectively. Threshold ECDSA for distributed key management produced two highly cited systems papers.

End-to-end encrypted messaging received formal treatment in 2019: SEEMless: Secure End-to-End Encrypted Messaging with less Trust (CCS 2019) introduced verifiable key transparency for messaging, and DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS (CCS 2020) extended TLS to enable users to prove data provenance to third parties without server cooperation, enabling smart-contract oracles. The 5G protocol stack was formally scrutinized in A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) and 5GReasoner (CCS 2019).

Consensus protocol research continued maturing through 2022 with Bullshark: DAG BFT Protocols Made Practical (CCS 2022), which achieved high throughput by building broadcast on a DAG rather than a linear chain. Dumbo-NG: Fast Asynchronous BFT Consensus with Throughput-Oblivious Latency (CCS 2022) separated throughput from latency in asynchronous settings.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice is dominated by two currents that the security community picked up almost simultaneously. One is scaling and securing distributed ledgers: OmniLedger (S&P 2018) and RapidChain (CCS 2018) both attacked the throughput ceiling of permissionless blockchains through sharding, while Arbitrum (USENIX 2018) tackled the same scalability wall from the smart-contract side. The other current is the machinery that makes such systems trustworthy — threshold and multiparty cryptography. Fast Multiparty Threshold ECDSA with Fast Trustless Setup and Secure Two-party Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions (both 2018) made splitting a signing key across parties practical, BEAT: Asynchronous BFT Made Practical (CCS 2018) pushed Byzantine consensus toward deployment, and General State Channel Networks (CCS 2018) laid groundwork for off-chain payments. Alongside these constructive results sat a strong strand of protocol breaking and formal analysis — The Dangers of Key Reuse: Practical Attacks on IPsec IKE (USENIX 2018) and the modelling of distance-bounding attacks (USENIX 2018) — establishing early that deployed crypto protocols needed adversarial scrutiny, not just proofs.

Over 2019–2020 the field matured along each of these lines. Cross-chain interoperability and payment scalability became first-class problems: XCLAIM (S&P 2019), Proof-of-Stake Sidechains (S&P 2019), and Perun: Virtual Payment Hubs over Cryptocurrencies (S&P 2019) built trustless bridges and payment hubs, later joined by A2L (S&P 2021). Consensus kept advancing with Flexible Byzantine Fault Tolerance (CCS 2019) and Sync HotStuff (S&P 2020). Crucially, the threshold-cryptography thread grew into a research program of its own — Towards Scalable Threshold Cryptosystems (S&P 2020) and Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation (CCS 2020) removed the trusted-dealer assumption that had blocked deployment. Formal analysis reached the protocols people actually use, most visibly in the Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA (NDSS 2019), and attack papers stayed prominent: Dragonblood (S&P 2020) broke WPA3's Dragonfly handshake, and Analysis of DTLS Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing (USENIX 2020) found flaws by systematically exercising real stacks. A notable new bridge appeared with DECO (CCS 2020), which used decentralized oracles to prove facts about TLS-protected web data, tying classical transport security to the blockchain world.

The 2022 papers consolidated the consensus and threshold agendas into their now-standard forms. Bullshark (CCS 2022) and Dumbo-NG (CCS 2022) showed that DAG-based, asynchronous BFT could be both fast and practical, while Practical Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation (S&P 2022) turned ADKG into a usable primitive. Universal Atomic Swaps (S&P 2022) generalized cross-chain exchange, and Eluding Secure Aggregation in Federated Learning (CCS 2022) extended the attack tradition into the privacy-preserving-ML setting, showing a supposedly secure aggregation protocol could be subverted by a malicious server.

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows the area settling into two mature fronts. Asynchronous consensus is still being refined for the best-of-both-worlds goal — Ipotane: Balancing the Good and Bad Cases of Asynchronous BFT and Icarus: Achieving Performant Asynchronous BFT with Only Optimistic Paths chase low latency without sacrificing worst-case guarantees, joined by Mobius (Byzantine-resilient secret leader election) and Cross-Consensus Reliable Broadcast. At the same time the classical transport-and-PKI agenda has re-energized under the quantum threat and Web3 demand: Looma: A Low-Latency PQTLS Authentication Architecture for Cloud Applications confronts post-quantum TLS handshakes, CTng and the SoK on Cryptographic Authenticated Dictionaries revisit certificate and revocation transparency, ACTS extends DECO's idea to attestations of TLS session contents, and efficient private-set primitives (cwPSU, Faster Than Ever PSI) round out the toolkit. The through-line from 2018 to 2026 is clear: the community keeps pairing new distributed-systems constructions with the threshold, PKI, and transport cryptography needed to make them trustworthy, while never letting go of adversarial analysis.
